title: 22. Interview: At Most Once Delivery
summary: Interview Q&A for At Most Once Delivery — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 At Most Once Delivery interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What does "at-most-once delivery" guarantee, and how does it differ from at-least-once?
**Answer:** At-most-once guarantees that each message is delivered zero or one times — never more than once, but possibly zero (silently lost). The producer fires the message and immediately moves on without waiting for an acknowledgment; the broker does not retain the message for redelivery; the consumer does not ack. If anything fails (broker down, network drop, consumer crash, slow consumer), the message is lost. At-least-once, by contrast, guarantees each message is delivered one or more times — never zero, but possibly more (duplicates). At-least-once uses acks (consumer acks after processing; broker redelivers if no ack) and message retention (broker holds the message until acked). The trade-off is: at-most-once has the lowest latency and zero ack overhead, but accepts losses; at-least-once has higher latency (ack round-trip) and ack overhead, but no losses (with duplicates possible). At-most-once is the right choice for low-value, high-volume, time-sensitive data (metrics, logs, telemetry) where losses are tolerable and latency matters; at-least-once is the right choice for high-value data (payments, orders, audit) where losses are unacceptable.
**Visual:**
```
at-most-once:  send -> broker -> consumer (no ack, loss possible)
at-least-once: send -> broker -> consumer -> ack (redeliver on no ack)
```

### Q2. Why use UDP for at-most-once, and what are the alternatives?
**Answer:** UDP is the natural transport for at-most-once because it is connectionless, has no built-in acknowledgment or retry, and has minimal per-packet overhead — a single UDP send is essentially a syscall and a network push, with no round-trip. This allows producers to fire hundreds of thousands of messages per second on a single thread. UDP is used by statsd, syslog, SNMP traps, collectd, and many monitoring pipelines. The alternatives are: (1) **TCP with `acks=0`**: Kafka's `acks=0` producer setting uses TCP for transport but does not wait for the broker's acknowledgment — combining TCP's reliable transport with at-most-once delivery semantics. (2) **HTTP fire-and-forget**: the producer POSTs to an endpoint and does not wait for the response (or uses async HTTP). This is used by some logging pipelines. (3) **In-memory queues**: for very high-volume, low-latency intra-process communication, an in-memory queue with no ack is effectively at-most-once (if the process crashes, the queue is lost). (4) **Shared memory or IPC**: for inter-process communication on the same host. The choice depends on the workload: UDP is best for high-volume, low-latency, network-tolerant metrics; TCP with `acks=0` is best when you need the broker's durability (e.g., Kafka) but can tolerate losses; HTTP fire-and-forget is best when integrating with HTTP-based systems. UDP's main drawback is no congestion control — under heavy load, UDP can flood the network and cause drops everywhere.
**Visual:**
```
UDP:           connectionless, no ack, no retry (statsd, syslog)
TCP acks=0:    reliable transport, no broker ack (Kafka)
HTTP async:    POST without waiting for response (logging pipelines)
in-memory:     no ack, no persistence (intra-process)
```

### Q3. What are the failure modes of at-most-once, and how do you mitigate them?
**Answer:** At-most-once has four main failure modes: (1) **Producer-broker failures**: if the broker is down when the producer sends, the message is lost. UDP producers often cannot even detect this (the OS just drops the packet). Mitigation: monitor broker availability; for TCP-based producers, the producer may detect connection failures but typically does not retry (to preserve at-most-once). (2) **Network drops**: UDP packets can be dropped by the network under congestion. Mitigation: provision enough bandwidth; monitor packet loss; consider TCP-based at-most-once if loss is too high. (3) **Consumer crashes**: if the consumer crashes mid-processing, the message is lost (no redelivery). Mitigation: keep processing fast and idempotent; minimize the crash window; consider checkpointing state periodically. (4) **Slow consumers / buffer overflow**: if the consumer cannot keep up, the broker's buffer fills and drops new messages (or oldest, depending on the drop policy). Mitigation: provision enough consumer capacity; monitor consumer lag; use an explicit drop policy (drop oldest is common for time-series data where stale data is useless; drop newest is common for alerting where missing the latest is worse than missing old). The system must be designed around these failures: monitor loss rates, set loss-rate SLOs (e.g., <0.1% loss acceptable), and alert if loss exceeds the SLO. For workloads where any of these failures is unacceptable, at-most-once is the wrong choice — use at-least-once.
**Visual:**
```
broker down:    msg LOST (UDP can't detect)
network drop:   msg LOST (no retry)
consumer crash: msg LOST (no ack, no redelivery)
slow consumer:  buffer overflow -> DROPPED (drop oldest/newest/random)
mitigation:     monitor loss rate, set SLO, provision capacity
```

### Q4. When is at-most-once the right choice, and when is it wrong?
**Answer:** At-most-once is right when ALL of the following hold: (1) Each individual message is low-value (losing 0.1% does not materially harm the system). (2) The aggregate is what matters, not individual messages (e.g., a metric's average over time). (3) Latency is critical (acknowledgment overhead would be unacceptable). (4) Volume is high (ack overhead per message would be prohibitive). (5) Stale data from delayed redelivery is worse than missing data (e.g., real-time signals). Classic examples: metrics (statsd), logs (UDP syslog), telemetry (collectd), real-time signals (gaming ticks, market data), IoT sensor streams. At-most-once is WRONG when ANY of the following hold: (1) Individual messages are high-value (payments, orders, audit logs — losing one is a bug). (2) The system relies on every message (e.g., a state machine that must process every event to stay consistent). (3) Loss is unacceptable for compliance or business reasons (financial transactions, healthcare records). (4) Latency is not critical (ack overhead is acceptable). The architect's rule: default to at-least-once for anything business-critical; downgrade to at-most-once only when you have explicitly justified that losses are tolerable and the latency/throughput benefit justifies the trade-off.
**Visual:**
```
RIGHT (at-most-once): metrics, logs, telemetry, real-time signals
WRONG (use at-least-once): payments, orders, audit, state machines
test: is losing 0.1% of messages acceptable? yes -> at-most-once OK
```

### Q5. How does Kafka's `acks=0` producer work, and what are its trade-offs?
**Answer:** Kafka's `acks=0` producer setting means the producer does not wait for the broker's acknowledgment — it considers the message "sent" as soon as it is handed to the network buffer. This gives the highest throughput (the producer can fire 100,000+ messages per second per thread) and the lowest latency (no round-trip wait), but it means the producer does not know if the broker received the message. If the broker is down, the network drops the packet, or the broker's buffer is full and rejects the message, the message is silently lost — the producer does not retry (or if it does, it may produce duplicates if the original actually went through). Compared to `acks=1` (wait for the leader's ack) and `acks=all` (wait for all in-sync replicas), `acks=0` has no durability guarantee. The trade-off is throughput/latency vs. reliability: `acks=0` is roughly 2-3x faster than `acks=1` and 5-10x faster than `acks=all`, but offers no delivery guarantee. Use `acks=0` for metrics, logs, and other low-value high-volume data; use `acks=1` for most business data (good balance); use `acks=all` for high-value data where durability is critical (payments, orders). Note that `acks=0` does not protect against broker-side issues either — if the leader is being elected, messages sent during the election are lost.
**Visual:**
```
acks=0:    send -> fire-and-forget (no ack, fastest, loss possible)
acks=1:    send -> wait for leader ack (balanced)
acks=all:  send -> wait for all ISR acks (slowest, most durable)
throughput: acks=0 > acks=1 > acks=all
durability: acks=all > acks=1 > acks=0
```

### Q6. How do you handle a slow consumer in an at-most-once pipeline?
**Answer:** A slow consumer in an at-most-once pipeline will eventually cause the broker's buffer to overflow, and the system must decide what to drop. Three common drop policies: (1) **Drop oldest** (most common for time-series data): when the buffer is full, the oldest message is evicted to make room for the new one. This is the right choice for metrics and telemetry where stale data is useless — you want the latest reading, not a 5-minute-old one. statsd and many metric pipelines use this implicitly via bounded queues. (2) **Drop newest** (common for alerting): when the buffer is full, the new message is dropped. This preserves older messages that the consumer will eventually process. Use this when missing the latest is worse than missing old (e.g., alerting where a missed alert is critical). (3) **Drop random**: randomly drop messages when the buffer is full. This gives an unbiased sample of the data, useful for analytics where you want a representative sample rather than the latest. Beyond the drop policy, the architect should: monitor consumer lag and alert if it grows; provision enough consumer capacity to handle peak load; consider sharding the consumer (more consumers in parallel) if a single consumer cannot keep up; consider downsampling at the producer (e.g., a statsd client that aggregates counters locally and sends every 10 seconds instead of every event). The drop policy should be a conscious choice, not an accident of buffer behavior.
**Visual:**
```
buffer full + drop oldest:  [m1][m2][m3] <- m4 drops m1 (stale data gone)
buffer full + drop newest:  [m1][m2][m3] <- m4 dropped (preserve history)
buffer full + drop random:  drop one of m1/m2/m3/m4 (unbiased sample)
```

### Q7. What real-world systems use at-most-once delivery?
**Answer:** Many high-volume, low-latency telemetry systems use at-most-once. **statsd** (from Etsy) is the canonical example: a UDP-based metrics aggregator that accepts metric packets with no ack and no retry — losing 0.1% of metric points is statistically insignificant for aggregation. **Collectd** and **Statsite** use similar UDP-based at-most-once for system metrics. **Syslog over UDP** (RFC 5426) is used by many logging pipelines for fire-and-forget log delivery — better to lose a log line than to block the application on log I/O. **SNMP traps** are sent over UDP with at-most-once semantics. **Netflix's Atlas** metrics pipeline supports at-most-once ingestion for high-volume metrics. **Datadog's agent** uses UDP for some metric types. **Kafka** with `acks=0` is used by some Kafka users for high-volume, low-value data. **Real-time signal pipelines**: gaming tick updates, financial market data feeds (e.g., NASDAQ ITCH over UDP multicast), and IoT sensor streams use at-most-once because stale data is worthless. **DNS** is effectively at-most-once over UDP — if a query is lost, the client times out and retries (which is at-most-once per attempt). The common theme: each individual message is low-value, the aggregate is what matters, latency is critical, and the volume is high enough that acknowledgment overhead would be prohibitive.
**Visual:**
```
statsd:        UDP metrics (lose 0.1% OK for aggregation)
syslog/UDP:    fire-and-forget logs (don't block app)
SNMP traps:    UDP network events
market data:   UDP multicast (stale = useless)
DNS:           UDP queries (client retries on timeout)
Kafka acks=0:  high-volume low-value data
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are designing a real-time metrics pipeline that ingests 1M metric points per second from 10,000 services. Latency must be <1ms. What delivery semantic do you use?
**Answer:** Use at-most-once delivery over UDP. The requirements (1M points/s, <1ms latency, 10,000 producers) make at-least-once infeasible: the ack round-trip alone would be 1-5ms per message, blowing the latency budget, and the broker's ack-handling capacity would need to handle 1M acks/s, which is expensive. At-most-once over UDP eliminates both: each producer fires a UDP packet (no round-trip), and the broker aggregates without acking. Losses are acceptable because metrics are aggregated (e.g., per-minute averages) — losing 0.1% of points does not materially change the aggregate, and the alarm thresholds are set with noise tolerance. Concretely: each service runs a statsd-like UDP sender (or a sidecar agent) that sends metric packets to a local aggregator; the aggregator batches and forwards to a time-series database (e.g., InfluxDB, Prometheus, TimescaleDB) over TCP with at-least-once (for the durable hop). The aggregation step naturally smooths over losses — a counter that should be 1000 might be 999 due to a lost packet, which is within noise. Monitor packet loss rates (via the broker's received-vs-expected count) and alert if loss exceeds 1% (indicates a real problem). The trade-off is explicit: low latency and high throughput at the cost of occasional losses, which is the right trade-off for metrics.
**Visual:**
```
10k services --UDP--> aggregators --TCP (at-least-once)--> TSDB
loss tolerance: <1% (aggregation smooths over it)
latency: <1ms per hop (no ack round-trip)
throughput: 1M points/s (no ack overhead)
```

### Q2. Your application logs are sent over UDP to a log aggregator. Under heavy load, you notice some log lines are missing. Is this acceptable, and how do you improve reliability?
**Answer:** Missing logs under heavy load are the expected behavior of at-most-once UDP — UDP packets are dropped under congestion, and the application does not retry. Whether this is acceptable depends on the log's purpose: for debug/trace logs, occasional loss is tolerable (the developer can reproduce the issue). For audit logs (security events, payment events), loss is unacceptable — switch to at-least-once (e.g., TCP syslog, or Kafka with `acks=all`). For application logs (errors, warnings), loss is borderline — losing an error log can hide a real problem. To improve reliability without abandoning at-most-once: (1) **Provision more bandwidth**: UDP drops are often due to network congestion; more bandwidth reduces drops. (2) **Increase buffer sizes**: tune the OS socket buffer (`sysctl net.core.rmem_max`) to absorb bursts. (3) **Add a local spool**: the application writes logs to a local file (durable) and a sidecar ships them via UDP; if UDP drops, the file retains the logs for later replay. (4) **Use TCP syslog**: if the application can tolerate slightly higher latency, TCP syslog with at-least-once is more reliable. (5) **Sample**: under heavy load, sample logs (send every Nth line) rather than dropping randomly — this preserves a representative sample. (6) **Monitor loss**: track the difference between sent and received logs, and alert if loss exceeds a threshold. The right answer depends on the log's business value — for audit, switch to at-least-once; for debug, keep at-most-once and accept the loss.
**Visual:**
```
audit logs:      switch to TCP syslog (at-least-once, durable)
error logs:      local spool + UDP ship (recover from file)
debug/trace:     keep UDP at-most-once (loss tolerable)
under heavy load: sample (every Nth) instead of random drop
```

### Q3. You are building a real-time gaming server that broadcasts player positions to all clients 30 times per second. Latency must be <50ms. What delivery semantic do you use?
**Answer:** Use at-most-once over UDP. The requirements (30 updates/s per player, <50ms latency, real-time) make at-least-once infeasible: TCP's head-of-line blocking would cause a single dropped packet to stall subsequent updates, blowing the latency budget; acks would add round-trips; redelivery of stale position data is useless (a 200ms-old position is meaningless when the player has moved). UDP with at-most-once is the standard for real-time multiplayer: if an update is lost, the client interpolates from the last received position, and the next update (33ms later) corrects any drift. Concretely: the server sends position updates as UDP packets (optionally with sequence numbers so the client can detect gaps); the client uses dead-reckoning or interpolation to smooth over missing updates; important events (player death, score changes) use a separate reliable channel (TCP or UDP with ack) to ensure delivery. This is exactly how games like Quake, Counter-Strike, and most modern multiplayer games work — the network protocol separates unreliable state updates (at-most-once) from reliable event messages (at-least-once). The trade-off is explicit: occasional visual stutter from lost updates is acceptable; high latency from TCP is not. The same pattern applies to financial market data, IoT sensor streams, and video streaming (WebRTC uses UDP with similar logic).
**Visual:**
```
position updates: UDP at-most-once (30/s, lose OK, interpolate)
events (death, score): TCP or UDP+ack (reliable, must arrive)
client: dead-reckoning between updates
lost update: client interpolates; next update corrects
```

### Q4. Your IoT device pipeline ingests temperature readings from 100,000 sensors every 10 seconds. Each sensor sends 1 reading per 10s. Do you use at-most-once or at-least-once?
**Answer:** Use at-most-once for the ingestion hop (sensor -> ingestion service), with at-least-once for the durable storage hop (ingestion -> database). The reasoning: 100,000 sensors * 1 reading per 10s = 10,000 readings/s, which is high volume but not extreme. The value of each individual reading is low (the temperature trend matters, not any single point). Sensors are often battery-powered and bandwidth-constrained, so the per-reading overhead of TCP+acks is significant. A lost reading every 10 seconds creates a 10-second gap in the time series, which can be interpolated. Concretely: sensors send readings via MQTT (QoS 0 = at-most-once) or UDP to an edge ingestion service; the ingestion service batches and writes to a time-series database (e.g., InfluxDB) over TCP with at-least-once (for durability — once ingested, the data must not be lost). If a sensor's reading is lost in transit, the time-series has a gap, which the dashboard can interpolate or flag. If the ingestion-to-DB hop fails, the data is lost (acceptable for a brief window) or buffered locally for retry. The trade-off is explicit: low-latency, low-power ingestion at the cost of occasional gaps, which are tolerable for temperature trends. For high-value sensors (e.g., safety-critical pressure sensors), use MQTT QoS 1 (at-least-once) end-to-end.
**Visual:**
```
sensor --MQTT QoS 0 (at-most-once)--> ingestion --TCP (at-least-once)--> TSDB
loss tolerance: occasional gaps (interpolated in dashboard)
power: low (no ack from sensor, no retransmit)
for safety-critical sensors: QoS 1 (at-least-once) end-to-end
```

### Q5. Your alerting pipeline triggers on a metric threshold (e.g., "error rate > 5%"). The metrics use at-most-once over UDP. Occasionally, alerts fire multiple times for the same threshold crossing. Why?
**Answer:** The duplicate alerts are caused by the alerting pipeline's evaluation logic interacting with at-most-once metric delivery. Specifically: (1) The metric aggregator receives UDP packets and computes the error rate; due to at-most-once, some error packets are lost, but enough get through that the rate exceeds 5%. (2) The alerting system evaluates the threshold every N seconds (e.g., every 10s) and triggers an alert; it then enters a "cooldown" period (e.g., 5 minutes) to prevent re-alerting. (3) If the cooldown is too short, the alert fires again after 5 minutes even though the underlying condition is the same. (4) More subtly, at-most-once metric delivery can cause the rate to fluctuate around 5% — one evaluation sees 4.8% (no alert), the next sees 5.2% (alert), the next sees 4.9% (no alert), then 5.5% (alert again). These fluctuations are amplified by the at-most-once loss: with fewer samples, the rate estimate is noisier. Fixes: (1) Increase the alert cooldown to prevent re-alerting on the same condition (e.g., 30 minutes). (2) Use a sustained threshold (e.g., "error rate > 5% for 2 minutes") to filter out noise. (3) Increase the metric sample size (aggregate over more data) to reduce noise. (4) Use at-least-once for the metric pipeline if the noise is unacceptable (e.g., for critical alerts). (5) Add alert deduplication in the alerting system (e.g., group alerts by metric+threshold within a window).
**Visual:**
```
UDP loss -> metric rate fluctuates: 4.8% / 5.2% / 4.9% / 5.5%
alerting: alert / no-alert / no-alert / alert (DUPLICATE!)
fix: sustained threshold (5% for 2 min) + cooldown (30 min)
```

### Q6. You are migrating a metrics pipeline from UDP (at-most-once) to Kafka (at-least-once). What changes, and what do you gain/lose?
**Answer:** The migration involves several changes: (1) **Producer**: switch from UDP send to Kafka producer with `acks=1` or `acks=all` and retries enabled. The producer's latency increases (from microseconds for UDP to single-digit milliseconds for Kafka with acks), and the producer must handle ack timeouts and retries. (2) **Consumer**: switch from UDP listener to Kafka consumer with manual offset commit (for at-least-once) — the consumer must be idempotent to handle duplicates from redelivery. (3) **Reliability**: gain — no more silent losses; every metric reaches the broker (assuming the broker is healthy). (4) **Latency**: lose — Kafka adds 1-5ms per message vs. UDP's microseconds, which may matter for real-time alerting. (5) **Throughput**: lose — Kafka's ack overhead caps the producer at perhaps 100k msg/s per thread vs. UDP's 1M+; you may need more producers or batching. (6) **Cost**: lose — Kafka is significantly more expensive (broker compute, storage, replication) vs. UDP (essentially free). (7) **Operational complexity**: lose — Kafka requires broker management, partitioning, monitoring, etc. vs. UDP's simplicity. (8) **Ordering**: gain — Kafka preserves partition ordering, which can be useful for per-host metric trends. The right choice depends on the workload: for low-volume, high-value metrics (e.g., business KPIs), the migration to Kafka is worth it; for high-volume, low-value metrics (e.g., per-request latency), UDP's simplicity and cost win. A hybrid is common: UDP for ingestion, Kafka for downstream processing.
**Visual:**
```
gain: reliability (no losses), ordering, durability
lose: latency (UDP us -> Kafka ms), throughput (1M -> 100k/s),
      cost (UDP free -> Kafka expensive), complexity
verdict: high-value metrics -> Kafka; high-volume -> UDP
```

### Q7. Your application uses at-most-once logging (UDP). A critical error log is lost, and the team cannot diagnose a production incident. How do you prevent this in the future?
**Answer:** The lost critical log reveals that at-most-once is inappropriate for high-value logs. The fix is to classify logs by criticality and use different delivery semantics: (1) **Critical logs (errors, security events, audit)**: switch to at-least-once via TCP syslog, Kafka with `acks=all`, or a synchronous file write (the application blocks until the log is durably written, accepting the latency cost for critical logs only). For audit logs, consider a transactional outbox pattern to ensure the log is durably persisted. (2) **Non-critical logs (debug, trace, info)**: keep at-most-once UDP — the latency benefit outweighs the occasional loss, and these logs are not needed for incident diagnosis. (3) **Hybrid**: the application writes all logs to a local file (durable, synchronous for critical, async for non-critical), and a sidecar (e.g., Filebeat, Fluentd) ships them via UDP (non-critical) or TCP (critical). This way, even if UDP drops a critical log, the file retains it for later replay. Concretely: (1) Implement a log-level-based routing in the application: errors and above go to a synchronous file write + TCP ship; info and below go to async file write + UDP ship. (2) Add monitoring on log delivery: track sent-vs-received counts per log level; alert if critical logs are lost. (3) Run a post-incident review to confirm the new setup would have caught the original incident. The lesson: at-most-once is a deliberate choice for low-value data; high-value data requires at-least-once, and the cost (latency, complexity) is justified by the value.
**Visual:**
```
critical logs:  sync file write + TCP ship (at-least-once, durable)
non-critical:   async file write + UDP ship (at-most-once, fast)
monitoring:     sent vs received per log level, alert on critical loss
post-incident:  confirm new setup catches the original incident
```
